questions.prompt: Which keyword prevents a class from being inherited from?
questions.explanation: `sealed` stops further derivation (and can also be applied to an `override` to stop it being overridden again). `final` is the Java equivalent and isn't a C# keyword. `static` classes are implicitly sealed, but that's a side effect, not their purpose.

`override` replaces the virtual method, so the runtime type (Dog) decides: "Dog speaks". `new` only *hides* the base method; it isn't polymorphic, so the compile-time type of the variable (Animal) decides: "Animal".

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between an abstract class and an interface in modern C#?
questions.answer: An abstract class can hold instance state and constructors, but a class can inherit only one; an interface has no instance state, and a class can implement many.
distractors: Interfaces cannot contain any method bodies; abstract classes can.
Abstract classes cannot have constructors; interfaces can.
There is no difference since C# 8; they are interchangeable.
questions.explanation: Since C# 8, interfaces *can* have default method implementations (and static members), so 'no method bodies' is outdated. The lasting differences: abstract classes can have instance fields and constructors and use single inheritance; interfaces can't hold instance state, and a class can implement many of them.
